summary:
On 22 April 2024 the High Court of Justice in Roseau held that sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act were unconstitutional insofar as they criminalised consensual same-sex activity between adults. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica. The court did not strike the sections down; it ordered them read down, so that section 14(2) exempts private consensual acts between adult persons who consent, and section 16(1)(b) exempts private consensual adult acts from the ten-year penalty for buggery. Both provisions remain on the statute book in that construed form.

The provisions the court construed were broad. The Sexual Offences Act 1998, as amended in 2016, criminalised male same-sex sexual activity and female same-sex sexual activity, and also anal intercourse between persons of the opposite sex. Section 14 punished gross indecency with 12 years' imprisonment where the complainant was 16 or older, and 14 years for a first offence or 20 years for a subsequent offence where the complainant was under 16, exempting only private consensual adult male-female acts. Section 16 punished buggery with 25 years where an adult committed it on a minor, 10 years where an adult committed it on another adult, 5 years where committed by a minor, and 4 years for attempt or assault with intent, and allowed the court to order admission to a psychiatric hospital for treatment.

The ruling addresses sexual conduct only. It creates no protection on grounds of gender identity or gender expression, and no Dominican law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Dominica gives no recognition to same-sex unions, whether as marriage or as civil unions, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no route to partner recognition, spousal immigration status or next-of-kin standing through a registered union.

Policing of anti-LGBT violence has been documented as dismissive. The man who filed the July 2019 constitutional challenge to the 10-year and 12-year provisions reported that police refused to investigate a violent attack on his home because, under Dominican law, gay people were considered criminals. A 2011 academic submission to the United Nations recorded that reports by victims to police were not taken seriously and that victims were sometimes ridiculed.

Violence against people perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming is documented, including a killing. In 2010 Clement James of Portsmouth was stabbed to death after being accused of "watching" his male assailant in a public place; the accused, Davis St Jean, was reported to preach in the street about killing gay people and to have said "all battie boi must dead" before the stabbing. Reporting on LGBTQ rights in Dominica also records suspected hate crimes against individuals believed to be homosexual, and the use of slurs such as "buggerman" and "battyman" for men read as effeminate.

Hostility has been directed at visitors specifically. In 2009 the president of the Evangelical Association, Bill Daniel, said "We want the government to ensure that gay tourists do not come to the island and conduct themselves in any immoral way"; the association protested gay cruises visiting the island and the promotion of Dominica as a gay tourist destination.

No available source documents the position of transgender people in Dominica specifically. There is no cited record of a trans-specific prosecution, a trans-specific violent incident, gender-marker or documentation rules, facility-access rules, or trans healthcare access. The 2024 judgment concerns consensual sexual conduct between adults and leaves gender identity, gender expression and gender-marker policy unaddressed by any cited instrument.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 ruling places Dominica among the jurisdictions of the Caribbean that have decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct by judicial decision. Human Rights Watch used its report on the case to call for repeal of comparable criminal laws across the Caribbean, which remain in force elsewhere in the region.

Dominica's delegation to the United Nations signed the 2011 joint statement to the Human Rights Council on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, one of 85 signatories. The commitment is dated and on the diplomatic record; it is not a domestic legal instrument and creates no enforceable protection.

Local religious authority has not uniformly supported the criminal provisions. In May 2013 Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica publicly called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for "all forms of violence" against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position.

The constitutional challenge was not sudden. On 20 July 2019 Dominica News Online reported that a High Court challenge to the buggery and sexual-activity laws had been filed by MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip and announced at a news conference, five years before the 2024 ruling.
localsOnly:
Enforcement of the pre-2024 provisions was not theoretical. Between 1995 and 2000 there were 35 arrests for buggery, resulting in fines and prison sentences of up to ten years, with some of those convicted sent to psychiatric hospitals for treatment. In 2001, 15 women were sentenced to five years for gross indecency and ten men were sentenced to five years for engaging in gross indecency with persons of the same sex.

In 2014 the Prime Minister said Dominica does not enforce its law against homosexual activity, at least in private homes, and had no plans to do so. That statement described enforcement practice rather than changing the statute, which remained in force until the 2024 reading-down.

Organised advocacy operates under pressure. A 2011 academic submission to the United Nations stated that LGBTQ groups in Dominica were forced to operate underground for fear that members would be victimised, and that openly gay members complained of vandalism against their property. Minority Rights Dominica (MiRiDom), founded by Darryl Philip, works as an LGBTQ advocacy group and brought the 2019 constitutional challenge.

The 2024 judgment concerns consensual sexual conduct between adults and does not address gender identity or expression.

The 2024 remedy is a reading-down, not a repeal. Sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act remain in the statute book in construed form, and no later appellate decision, legislative amendment or government statement confirming how the provisions will be applied going forward is sourced here.

The material on underground organising, property vandalism and dismissive police responses to victims comes from a 2011 academic submission to a United Nations body rather than from a government record or court finding, and its currency is unresolved.
